::: {.why}
The headline results in this literature are real and much smaller than the abstracts suggest, and being able to convert them into your own units is what stops you from either dismissing or overestimating them.
:::

## What you should be able to do tonight

- Convert two published results into information ratio at a stated breadth and compare against your own models.
- Name the methodological choice in each paper that most affects its headline number.

## Tasks <span class='task-total'>60 min</span>

::: {.task-list}
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [35 min]{.task-min} Read both papers' results sections and tabulate: sample period, universe, features, out-of-sample metric and its value, and the portfolio performance they report. Then convert each into the units you use and put your own models in the same table.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [25 min]{.task-min} Find the choice that drives each result: usually the feature set rather than the architecture, and often the inclusion of microcaps where the returns are large and untradeable. Check whether either paper reports results with a liquidity screen, and note what happens to the headline when they do.
:::
:::

## Resources

- [Chen, Pelger & Zhu — Deep Learning in Asset Pricing](https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.00745) [paper]{.res-kind}
- [Gu, Kelly & Xiu (2020) — Empirical Asset Pricing via Machine Learning](https://dachxiu.chicagobooth.edu/download/ML.pdf) [paper]{.res-kind}

## Deliverable

::: {.deliverable}
A comparison table putting two published results and your own models in the same units, with the driving methodological choice named for each.
:::

## Checkpoint

::: {.checkpoint}
A paper reports a monthly out-of-sample R-squared of 0.4 percent. What information ratio is that at 500 names, and does it survive a liquidity screen?
:::
